detail.abstract: What are the equilibrium and welfare effects of delegating decision-making to large language models (LLMs)? We study this question by comparing human and LLM-generated purchase choices around the introduction of menu labeling laws in a major restaurant market. We find that menu labeling had limited effects on calorie intake. By contrast, delegating purchase decisions to ChatGPT would reduce total calorie intake by up to 18%. Delegation also induces substantial exit of unsold product varieties and increases market concentration. We develop a structural model of delegation to quantify the underlying mechanisms and welfare effects. The net effect of delegation on total welfare is positive but has important distributional consequences: consumer surplus rises substantially for those who delegate to large language models, while the surplus of non-delegating consumers declines slightly due to equilibrium effects. Firm profits also increase.

detail.abstract: This study relies on NielsenIQ data from 2020 and computes a food purchase sustainability index (FPsi) for households in the United states based on three dimensions-environmental, nutritional, and economic. a household-level score is calculated for each of the three dimensions, and 26 indicators are used to construct the final FPsi. i aggregate household-level indices to derive an overall state-level FPsi and show how findings differ across states, separately for environmental (eNPs), nutritional (NPs), and economic purchase scores (ePs). i use multiple linear regression to assess the strength of the correlation between various household demographics and the FPsi. the analysis reveals stark differences in the overall FPsi across states; these differences extend to environmental footprints, nutritional quality, and affordability of food purchases. i find Maryland and Wyoming are the highest-ranking states in overall FPsi, with higher scores indicating greater overall sustainability. No state ranks the highest across all dimensions. idaho and Oklahoma are the lowest-ranking states; thus, targeted interventions could yield the most significant improvements in sustainability metrics in those two states. these results advance sustainable Development Goal 12 (Responsible consumption and Production) by addressing socioeconomic disparities in sustainability outcomes across households in the United states and individual states, providing evidence to support targeted, region-specific policymaking. the FPsi and its sub-scores enable researchers and policymakers to identify the states requiring the timeliest interventions in each dimension, and to track temporal shifts in sustainability levels.

title: Value-Based Consumer Behavior and Store Loyalty: Evidence from Generation Z in Turkey’s Hard-Discount Retail Sector
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Value-Based Consumer Behavior and Store Loyalty: Evidence from Generation Z in Turkey’s Hard-Discount Retail Sector
detail.abstract: This study investigates how value awareness among Generation Z consumers drives loyalty toward private label products in Turkey’s hard-discount retail sector. Building on Social Exchange Theory (SET), the research conceptualizes store loyalty as an outcome of relational exchange processes shaped by cognitive evaluations and socio-psychological mechanisms. Specifically, the study examines the mediating roles of customer satisfaction and store trust in linking value awareness to loyalty. Empirical data were collected from 1,505 Generation Z consumers and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that value awareness significantly enhances both customer satisfaction and store trust. However, its effect on store loyalty is fully indirect, operating through a sequential mechanism in which satisfaction strengthens trust, which in turn drives loyalty. The findings confirm that trust is the most critical determinant of loyalty in value-driven retail contexts. This study extends SET by demonstrating that value-based consumer behavior is not purely economic but is embedded in relational and psychological processes that evolve through satisfaction and trust formation. The findings provide actionable implications for retailers in emerging markets, highlighting the importance of delivering consistent value, strengthening trust-building mechanisms, and enhancing satisfaction to sustain Generation Z loyalty toward private labels in competitive retail environments.

title: AI Innovation Architecture: Nested Purpose, Closed-Loop Dynamics, and the Chief Agency Officer

detail.title: AI Innovation Architecture: Nested Purpose, Closed-Loop Dynamics, and the Chief Agency Officer
detail.abstract:
The AI revolution confronts every organisation with a stark imperative: maximise the rate of innovation per unit time, or face accelerating obsolescence (Dixon, 2025d). As organisations embed AI into their operations, AI systems are no longer merely tools; they are becoming agents that set sub-purposes, run optimisation loops, and shape organisational direction. The question of who sets purpose, who executes, who judges, and how agency is progressively delegated becomes the defining architectural challenge of the AI era.

The structural language is provided by the Purpose, Execution, Judgement (PEJ) framework (Dixon, 2026b). This paper first establishes a dual operating model: business as usual (BAU), optimised for return on investment, and Innovation, optimised to maximise the rate of innovation per unit time, proposing an 85 per cent (BAU) to 15 per cent (Innovation) initial resource allocation target. It then defines agency within PEJ as a scale rather than a binary, always bounded by Purpose above and Judgement below, and extends PEJ into a nested, multidimensional model involving varying configurations of human and AI actors in both open and closed loops.

Seven original contributions address how an organisation structures and optimises this system: a formal definition of agency and the agentic scale; nested multi-dimensional PEJ with purpose leakage as the dynamic pathology; topological consistency of purpose; the purpose-method boundary; closed-loop innovation with three trajectories and loop hygiene; the Chief Agency Officer within a reoriented C-suite structured around the dual operating model; and the Child Emperor trajectory. Ten formal propositions are advanced for empirical testing.

title: From SEO to AIO (II): Category Moderation and the Refinement of Operational Dominance in the Agent Decision Preference Stack

detail.title: From SEO to AIO (II): Category Moderation and the Refinement of Operational Dominance in the Agent Decision Preference Stack
detail.abstract: Accornero (2025) introduced the Agent Decision Preference Stack and reported a 4.71x operational dominance ratio from a single-category simulation of AI-mediated product selection. This paper extends that finding through a comprehensive nine-study computational program spanning over 1,000 simulated markets across ten product categories. We demonstrate that the original 4.71x ratio was a valid observation for its specific dataset and configuration but is not a universal constant. Extended testing reveals a mean operational dominance ratio of approximately 1.24x (Cohen's d = 0.50-0.78), with 65-79% of simulated markets exhibiting operational advantage. For simulation purposes, the Inferred Knowledge layer (L2) is operationalised through brand-related attributes, and the Real-Time Optimization layer (L3) through operational attributes including price, delivery speed, and availability. We introduce the Category Moderation Effect: the magnitude of operational dominance within the Preference Stack is moderated by market size, agent decision architecture, and agent weight configuration, though notably not by product category. One-way ANOVA across categories yields F(9, 990) = 1.18, p = .306, η2 = .011, indicating that the operational advantage is a universal property of algorithmic multi-attribute evaluation: robust and consistent across categories, with no significant variation in magnitude between them. These findings validate the three-layer Preference Stack architecture while refining its quantitative predictions, producing a stronger and more defensible theoretical contribution.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how cybersecurity professionals integrate Foundation AI (FAI) systems into their workflows, examining perceptions, new behaviors, and the dynamics of human control. Drawing on expert interviews with 20 cybersecurity professionals, the research identifies key thematic factors that shape human-FAI configurations at work, including professional experience and reliability concerns. Findings reveal that FAI adoption entails shared control arrangements wherein decision-making power is continuously exchanged in a human-FAI entanglement, but humans retain final authority over critical decisions. However, adoption frequently outpaces the development of systematic risk mapping or control processes, creating operational tensions wherein practitioners must navigate FAI integration through trialand-error experimentation and resulting in highly idiosyncratic workflows that vary considerably across individuals and teams. Given the limited accessibility of expert cybersecurity practitioners, this study provides an empirical contribution to understanding FAI adoption dynamics, addressing a research gap at the intersection of FAI adoption and cybersecurity practice.

detail.abstract: Insurance operations generate continuous streams of regulated state transitions-policy issuance, claim adjudication, premium collection, broker remittance-that must be auditable for years and verifiable on demand by regulators, reinsurance counterparties, and litigation adversaries. The prevailing industry practice protects these audit trails through database access controls and policy-based logging in mutable relational stores. This approach is insufficient: it requires regulators to trust the platform vendor, exposes Personally Identifiable Information (PII) during inspection, and provides no mathematical defense against retrospective tampering by privileged insiders or attackers with database access. This paper introduces the Regure Immutable Audit (RIA) Protocol, a cryptographic statetransition anchoring system that organizes insurance operational events into per-tenant Merkle trees, signs each daily root with a tenant-specific hardware-backed key via AWS Key Management Service, and anchors the signed root to two independent immutable witnesses: AWS S3 Object Lock and the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps. Verification is implemented as a zero-knowledge protocol: an external auditor can verify the cryptographic integrity of any specific event in any specific claim using a Merkle proof of length 𝑂(log 𝑛)against a publicly anchored root, without ever observing the underlying claim data. We provide formal definitions of the State-to-Hash Mapping, the Hash-Linked Lifecycle property, and the Dual-Witness Anchoring Construction. We prove that the system is tamper-evident under standard cryptographic assumptions, that verification has logarithmic complexity in the number of events per tenant per day, and that the Zero-Knowledge Audit property holds against both honest-but-curious regulators and an actively malicious platform vendor. We describe the production implementation deployed in Cryptographic State-Transition Anchoring Piyoosh Rai P a g e | 2 Regure, including the integration with AWS KMS for tenant-isolated signing keys and the dual anchoring path through Object Lock storage and Bitcoin transaction confirmation. We discuss the implications for Continuous Assurance under DORA Article 12, the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP), the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) Cyber Security Framework, and Lloyd's market reporting requirements for delegated authority operations. The RIA Protocol moves the insurance industry's audit trust model from "trusting the vendor" to "trusting the math"-a structural shift that resolves the long-standing conflict between the regulatory Right to Audit and the data subject's right to privacy.

detail.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly depend on complex digital systems to manage enrollment, financial aid, research administration, and institutional reporting. As these systems expand, data governance is often treated as a technical or administrative function rather than a strategic institutional capability. However, recent compliance challenges, reporting inconsistencies, and audit findings suggest that weak governance frameworks can introduce significant institutional risk. This paper argues that data governance should be understood not merely as an internal operational concern but as a form of institutional infrastructure essential to the integrity, accountability, and sustainability of higher education systems. The study examines how fragmented data structures, unclear stewardship responsibilities, and inconsistent governance frameworks can undermine regulatory compliance, accreditation credibility, and public trust. Drawing on institutional governance principles and information systems perspectives, the paper proposes a risk-informed view of data governance that emphasizes cross-domain coordination, clear accountability structures, and system-wide data standards. By reframing governance as foundational infrastructure rather than a supporting function, institutions can better mitigate systemic risks and strengthen the reliability of institutional data used in federal reporting, accreditation processes, and strategic decision-making. The paper concludes that effective data governance is critical not only for operational efficiency but also for maintaining transparency, accountability, and resilience within U.S. higher education systems.

title: Le Bureau des Légendes: A Dynamic Theory of Double Agents
affiliations: Department of Economics and

detail.title: Le Bureau des Légendes: A Dynamic Theory of Double Agents
detail.abstract: This paper models double agents-individuals coerced into simultaneously serving two rival intelligence agencies-as a finite-horizon trilateral game between Agency A, Organization B, and the Mole M. The double agent persists within a corridor of survival : a set of bilateral beliefs under which both principals continue the relationship. Under a linear-quadratic-Gaussian benchmark, we obtain a closed-form characterization of the corridor geometry, analytical upper bounds on expected duration, and three main results: (i) existence of a double-agent equilibrium, (ii) structural transitorinessbelief updating, terminal unraveling, and compounding survival risk ensure inevitable collapse, and (iii) comparative statics linking monitoring technology, punishment severity, and protection costs to expected duration. The key mechanism is self-destructive experimentation: B learns about the mole's type through both the type-dependence of effort and the traceability channel γ, which amplifies this learning. Extensions establish existence under general specifications and show that duration decays exponentially in the number of rival agencies. Predictions are consistent with historical patterns from Kim Philby to the Cold War mole hunts. The setting-bilateral coercion, existential participation constraints, and Bayesian learning in a finite-horizon trilateral structuredefines what we term antagonistic common agency.

title: Causal Agency: A Persistence-Control Theory of Adaptive Systems

detail.title: Causal Agency: A Persistence-Control Theory of Adaptive Systems
detail.abstract: Agency is a central concept across philosophy of action, cognitive science, theoretical biology, and artificial intelligence. Despite extensive research across these fields, existing accounts remain theoretically fragmented because they are typically grounded in domain-specific mechanisms and operate at different explanatory levels. Philosophical theories emphasize intentional action and rational deliberation, biological theories focus on metabolic self-maintenance, and computational models define agents primarily in terms of goal-directed decision processes. While each of these perspectives captures important aspects of agency, none provides a structural account capable of explaining agency across the full spectrum of adaptive systems. This paper proposes a structural theory of agency based on a persistence-control framework. Within this framework, systems are interpreted as dynamical systems operating under constraint structures that shape the possible trajectories of their states. Persistence is defined as the continued occupation of a viable region of state space that allows the system to maintain its organization or functional identity. Agency emerges when the internal dynamics of a system are capable of regulating or modifying the constraint structures that govern its own persistence. By defining agency in terms of constraint-modulating dynamics, the framework shifts the explanation of agency away from particular biological, cognitive, or computational mechanisms toward the structural conditions that enable adaptive systems to regulate their own trajectories. This perspective provides a domain-general account applicable to biological organisms, cognitive agents, and artificial systems. The paper develops the conceptual foundations of the persistence-control framework, introduces a minimal formal representation, and analyzes its relationship to existing theories of biological autonomy, predictive processing, and artificial agency. It argues that agency should be understood as a graded structural phenomenon that emerges through increasingly complex forms of persistence regulation across adaptive systems.

detail.abstract: Research on digital information manipulation overwhelmingly focuses on adversarial actors engaged in propaganda, disinformation, and strategic narrative manipulation. Consequently, most analytical frameworks assume that coordinated shaping of the information environment is inherently malicious. This paper challenges that assumption by introducing the concept of Benevolent Information Ecosystem Manipulation (BIEM)-the deliberate shaping of digital information environments by legitimate institutional actors with the goal of mitigating conflict escalation or reducing the salience of inflammatory narratives. Using a conceptual detection architecture called KAIROS (Knowledge Authority Integrity and Retrieval Origin System), this study evaluates whether existing influence-operation detection methodologies can distinguish between adversarial propaganda campaigns and institutional conflict-prevention interventions. Through a simulated comparative case study, the analysis examines a hypothetical United Nations conflict-prevention intervention and compares its operational signature against documented adversarial influence operations. The results reveal significant structural ambiguity: detection systems classify both scenarios as coordinated influence operations with high confidence. This finding reveals a critical limitation-Detection Ambiguity Risk-the probability that automated information integrity systems misclassify legitimate institutional interventions as hostile manipulation. The paper proposes a two-layer analytical framework incorporating structural detection and normative evaluation, and introduces five governance principles for institutional information ecosystem interventions.

title: The Trinity Value Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Trinity Value Framework
detail.abstract: Organizations operating in the age of Agentic AI must simultaneously create three structurally distinct forms of value-functional, institutional, and security-while navigating environments characterized by increasing uncertainty and distributed information. The Trinity Value Framework (TVF) proposes that organizational failure rarely results from insufficient resources or capabilities. Instead, failure emerges when an organization's Dominant Logic leads it to misdefine the underlying scarcity it must address. Because problem definitions determine which coordination mechanisms organizations employ-whether markets, hierarchies, platforms, or AI-mediated systems-misdefined problems systematically generate misaligned coordination architectures and distorted learning processes. The framework therefore connects environmental uncertainty, information processing, problem definition, coordination mechanism choice, and value creation within a single integrative model. The framework further specifies the leadership actions required to interrupt this failure cycle: redefining the problem narrative, making coordination mechanism selection explicit, and redesigning organizational feedback architecture to close the learning loop across all three value dimensions. The argument is illustrated through the Volkswagen Dieselgate case and applied to three pressing industry contexts: the automotive transition, the German healthcare system, and the energy transformation.

detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential in healthcare management, yet their inherent context window limitation prevents sustained cross-session cognitive continuity-a critical deficiency in elderly health management scenarios where safety-critical health facts must be retained over extended periods. Adopting a Design Science Research methodology and drawing on the case of "Zang Xiaoxiang" (藏小象 , literally "Visceral Little Elephant," referencing the Zang-fu organ system in Traditional Chinese Medicine), a preventive health management system for middle-aged and elderly users, this paper presents a healthsafety-aware long-term memory architecture. Key contributions include: (1) a four-dimensional stratified memory space model separating working memory, health profile memory, procedural memory, and system constraint memory; (2) a health-safety-priority memory classification scheme where safety-critical constraint memories are never automatically degraded; (3) precompression memory flush and urgent keyword extraction mechanisms ensuring safety information preservation; and (4) hot/cold path separation for computational cost control. Following Hevner et al.'s (2004) design science principles, this paper contributes the architectural artifact rather than large-scale empirical validation.

title: Socially Embedded LLMs as Social Facilitators: Evidence from a Natural Experiment on X.com
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Socially Embedded LLMs as Social Facilitators: Evidence from a Natural Experiment on X.com
detail.abstract: The integration of generative AI (Gen-AI) into social platforms is fundamentally reshaping how users discover information and interact online. This study examines an emerging class of platform native generative systems we term Socially Embedded LLMs (SELs), which draw on real-time user content to synthesize contextual responses and route user attention back into the platform's social graph. We analyze the release of Grok on X.com, introduced to non-premium users in New Zealand in November 2024, but not elsewhere. Exploiting this release, we employ a difference-indifferences (DID) design using Australia as the control group. Results show that Grok increases engagement with others' posts (favorites, replies, and reposts) by lowering discovery barriers and providing interaction-ready entry points to real-time content. These effects are most pronounced for low-popularity topics, suggesting that SELs can revitalize the "longtail" of discussions. Mechanism analyses further suggest that Grok enhances engagement, in part, by increasing participant and topic diversity, thereby attracting broader audiences and fostering conversations across topical clusters. These findings provide early causal evidence that, when designed with embedded social entry points, SELs function as facilitators rather than information substitutes, highlighting their potential to rebalance attention and strengthen the resilience of social media ecosystems.

Improving Participation in Digital Feedback Applications: Social Norms Appeals in Technology Management 
Forthcoming at Production and Operations Management
detail.abstract: Real-time feedback applications are reshaping employee performance feedback in operations management. Their design and implementation significantly influence employee engagement, which is a key factor in the success of technology-driven business innovations. This study investigates an implementation strategy to optimize feedback app use by employing digital nudges to encourage regular engagement. Drawing on social norms theory and cognitive load theory, we examine how message framing and users' cognitive states affect the quantity and content features of feedback, including ratings, review length, surprise, and recognition. We conducted two randomized experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of digital nudges. Experiment 1, a field study with over 250 users of the DevelapMe app in a financial firm, tested how message framing and timing influenced cognitive load. Experiment 2, an online randomized controlled trial, explored underlying mechanisms and validated cognitive load measures. The results show that while social norms-based nudges increase feedback volume, they are associated with shorter reviews and reduced recognition and surprise. Employees experiencing lower cognitive load provided more feedback but tended to give lower ratings. Importantly, the interaction between social norms and low cognitive load resulted in higher ratings and more detailed reviews. This suggests that reducing cognitive load can enhance the positive effects of social norms on feedback quality. This study underscores the moderating role of cognitive load in the effectiveness of digital nudges and offers insights into feedback design that promotes both participation and quality. Theoretically, it contributes to research on digital feedback systems by integrating social norms and cognitive load theories to explain employee feedback behavior. Practically, it provides guidance for managers in designing real-time feedback tools that strategically use digital nudges while minimizing cognitive load, fostering a culture of continuous feedback, strengthening engagement, and improving performance management systems.

title: Beyond the Productivity Narrative: Artificial Intelligence, the Infinite Problem Space, and the Enduring Role of Human Agency

detail.title: Beyond the Productivity Narrative: Artificial Intelligence, the Infinite Problem Space, and the Enduring Role of Human Agency

detail.abstract: The dominant discourse around artificial intelligence and employment centers on a simple and commercially useful claim: workers who adopt AI tools will outcompete those who do not. This paper argues that framing is incomplete at best and misleading at worst. While AI literacy may extend individual relevance in the near term, the deeper transformation is structural rather than ergonomic. AI represents the first technology in history to externalize not a specific physical or logistical capability, but reasoning itself-the faculty previously assumed to be uniquely and safely human. This distinction matters. Rather than a familiar cycle of job displacement and re-employment, AI is likely to compress the timeline of technological progress so dramatically that it generates entirely new categories of problems faster than previous solutions can settle. These upstream problems-definitional, ethical, prioritizational-require human agency to pose before any machine can be pointed at them. The paper further argues that the commonly feared dystopia of human obsolescence misunderstands the nature of the problem space. From unsolved diseases to energy constraints, from space exploration to the basic governance of intelligent systems, the frontier of consequential problems is not shrinking. It is expanding. The question is not whether humans will be replaced. It is what kind of work humans will do next-and why that work will remain, structurally and permanently, beyond the reach of any tool that cannot want anything.

title: Artificial Adaptive Systems
affiliations: The Unicist Research Institute

detail.title: Artificial Adaptive Systems
detail.abstract:
Artificial adaptive systems are autonomous entities designed to operate within dynamic environments by
emulating the functional structure that underlies natural adaptive systems. Their behavior is regulated
by a triadic architecture composed of purpose, active function, and energy conservation function, which
defines their capacity to sustain functionality over time. In this context, “being alive” refers to
maintaining operational continuity while preserving autonomy and the ability to self-organize.

These systems operate with open boundaries, enabling continuous interaction with their environment
through the exchange of information and feedback. Their functionality is inherently feedback-
dependent, meaning that the value of their actions is validated within the unified field in which they
participate. This unified field integrates the system with its restricted and wide contexts, defining the
conditions under which it can operate and evolve.

The operational dynamics of artificial adaptive systems are driven by binary actions, which translate their
underlying functionalist principles into effective interventions. These synchronized actions allow the
system to influence its environment while managing the reactions generated, ensuring the achievement
of outcomes. As outcome-driven entities, their functionality is ultimately defined by the results they
produce and the validation of these results within their context.

The reliability of these systems is established through unicist destructive tests, which determine the
limits of their functionality by expanding their application beyond initial boundaries. This validation
approach replaces traditional falsification by defining the range of validity of the system’s behavior.
Overall, artificial adaptive systems provide a causal framework that integrates conceptual structure and
operational execution, enabling the management of functionality, dynamics, and evolution in complex
environments.

detail.title: Structuring Real-World Asset Tokenisation: A Lifecycle Framework for Corporate Lawyers
detail.abstract: Real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation has matured as a critical interface between blockchain technology and established legal-financial infrastructures. As of March 2026, on-chain tokenised RWAs exceed $26 billion in distributed value, nearly quadrupling year-over-year, driven by institutional adoption in the U.S. Treasuries, private credit, funds, and emerging sectors, with projections anticipating multi-trillion-dollar scales by the early 2030s. While technical mapping of off-chain assets or revenue rights to on-chain tokens is increasingly robust, the legal implications remain fragmented and undertheorised. Amid 2025-2026 regulatory shifts, such as the enactment of the U.S. GENIUS Act and advancement of the CLARITY Act, this framework gains urgency for ensuring compliance and enforceability in a maturing market. This article sees RWA tokenisation as an ongoing legal infrastructure project rather than a purely technological or financial innovation. It advances a lifecycle-based analytical framework to guide company lawyers in designing, structuring, and sustaining legally enforceable tokenised assets across initiation, structuring, issuance, operation, and liquidation stages. Drawing on representative case studies from energy, infrastructure, and agricultural sectors, the analysis examines how tokenisation reshapes securities characterisation, property-rights enforcement, cross-border structuring, and regulatory compliance. It surveys approaches in leading jurisdictions, such as the US, Hong Kong, Singapore, and UEA, emphasising sandboxes, institutional coordination, and technology-neutral supervision in managing legal risk. The article contends that long-term viability depends more on sustained legal and regulatory stability than on technological scalability. By integrating doctrinal analysis with market practice, it clarifies the central role of corporate lawyers as architects of resilient structures that bridge traditional finance and decentralised systems amid accelerating institutional momentum and regulatory maturation.

detail.abstract: ESG ratings increasingly govern index construction and investment mandates, creating a conflict of interest for investor-paid raters: because rating changes trigger rebalancing costs for subscribers, raters face pressure to favor stability over timeliness. We document a traffic light effect at MSCI, the world’s largest ESG rater: companies systematically bunch just below letter-rating thresholds, as if queued behind a red light. By reverse-engineering MSCI’s benchmarking methodology, we identify committee adjustments that create wedges between methodology-implied and published scores. These wedges grow with divergence from peer consensus, especially when peers agree closely, consistent with a model in which investor-paid raters trade methodological consistency for peer alignment. Exploiting a methodology change at Refinitiv, we show that MSCI conditions overrides on contemporaneously available peer ratings rather than on common fundamentals. Implemented downgrades predict negative returns of 2.8% over twelve months; suppressed downgrades do not.

detail.abstract: Linguistic uncertainty is a common feature of social media discourse, yet its relationship with user engagement remains underexplored, particularly in non-English contexts. Using a dataset of 16,695 Arabic-language tweets about Lebanon posted over a 35-day period, we examine whether tweets expressing linguistic uncertainty receive different levels and forms of engagement compared to certainty-marked tweets. We develop a lexicon-based, context-sensitive classifier to identify uncertainty markers and classify 29.9% of tweets as uncertain. Descriptive analyses indicate that uncertain tweets exhibit 51.5% higher mean total engagement (likes, retweets, and replies). Regression models controlling for tweet length, URL presence, and account verification status confirm a positive association between uncertainty and engagement (β = 0.221, SE = 0.044, p < 0.001), corresponding to approximately 25% higher expected engagement. The association is strongest for replies, followed by retweets and likes, suggesting a shift toward more conversational forms of engagement. Results are robust to alternative model specifications and adjustments for within-account correlation. These findings suggest that linguistic uncertainty may function as an interactional cue that encourages participatory engagement in Arabic-language social media discourse. The study contributes computational approaches for modeling linguistic features in large-scale, non-English digital communication.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in financial decision systems, yet a fundamental limitation persists: models may generate outputs that are statistically coherent while remaining structurally invalid. This paper reframes AI hallucination not as a computational anomaly or data deficiency, but as a causal failure—a breakdown in the structural representation of how financial outcomes are generated through decisions, behavior, and temporal propagation.

The study argues that conventional expected-value and probability-based reasoning compress heterogeneous causal pathways into averaged representations, obscuring structurally significant scenarios and masking low-probability, high-impact risks. Such compression contributes to model fragility and amplifies the likelihood of AI hallucination within financial systems.

To address this, the paper introduces a causal-analytical framework based on the decision → behavior → time → effect chain, enabling identification of structural inconsistencies within financial models, including localized breakdowns termed causal failure points (hallucination nodes). It further proposes scenario-complete reasoning as an alternative to distribution-dominant modelling, emphasizing explicit representation of central and extreme causal trajectories.

By integrating causal inference, AI governance, and financial decision theory, this work advances a structural shift from prediction-centric modelling toward causally grounded financial decision systems. The framework offers implications for AI reliability, financial model validation, risk management, and regulatory oversight in increasingly AI-driven financial environments.

detail.abstract:
Background: Extreme heat poses growing risks to human health, particularly in low-and middle income countries (LMICs) where exposure is high and adaptive capacity is often limited. While a range of interventions have been proposed to reduce heat-related health impacts, the evidence base on their effectiveness in LMIC contexts remains fragmented. 

Objectives: This scoping review systematically maps the existing literature on interventions aimed at reducing adverse health impacts of heat in LMICs, examining the types of interventions studied, targeted populations, health outcomes assessed, and the methods used to evaluate impacts. 

Methods: Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, we conducted literature searches in December 2025 across Embase, Global Health, Global Index Medicus, PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar and Elicit, complemented by reverse citation searches. We included peer-reviewed and gray literature assessing interventions related to heat exposure and reporting health or health-related outcomes in LMIC settings. 

Results: We identified 103 studies covering eight intervention categories: building and housing adaptations (37), personal cooling strategies (19), occupational heat protection (18), health system and social protection programs (17), heat warning and preparedness (17), behavioral heat protection (13), landscape heat mitigation (12), and cooling infrastructure (6). Studies are heavily concentrated in Asia, particularly China and India, with limited evidence from Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. Many studies evaluate intermediate outcomes, such as indoor temperature, while relatively few assess morbidity and mortality. Experimental methods are common but are typically conducted in controlled, short-term settings, limiting insights into real-world behavioral responses, adoption barriers, and intervention effectiveness. 

Conclusion: Evidence on heat adaptation interventions for health in LMICs remains fragmented and uneven across regions and intervention types. Robust evaluations of real-world interventions, particularly those targeting vulnerable populations and long-term health outcomes, are scarce. Addressing these gaps will be critical for informing effective policies to reduce heat-related health risks in vulnerable settings. * Acknowledgments: We are grateful for comments and suggestions from the audience at the Energy, Environment and Development seminar at Duke University.

detail.abstract: Psychological distress is commonly conceptualised as an individual phenomenon arising from biological vulnerability, maladaptive cognition, or psychiatric disorder. While these factors are important, they do not adequately explain why similar stressors produce markedly different outcomes across individuals. This paper argues that distress is relationally mediated and context-dependent, emerging from interactions between individual vulnerability, internal regulatory states, and relational environments. The paper introduces the Social Buffer Hypothesis, which proposes that relational environments function as regulatory systems that either attenuate or amplify distress through their effects on emotional regulation capacity and perceived agency. Supportive environments stabilise internal states through co-regulation, meaning reconstruction, and reinforcement of agency, whereas invalidating or anxious environments intensify dysregulation and contribute to escalation of distress. A Social Injury Framework is further developed to account for structural and institutional sources of harm, including discrimination, exclusion, humiliation, and institutional betrayal. These experiences disrupt regulation, meaning, and agency, increasing vulnerability to amplification processes. A conceptual model of social amplification and buffering pathways is presented, followed by clinical and policy implications. The paper advances a relational-ecological model of mental health, reframing distress as a function of dynamic interactions between internal states and social environments rather than solely individual pathology.

title: The Fear Response Gap: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding Behavioral Adaptation to Chronic Stress in Indigenous Communities

detail.abstract: The Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE) Study established a graded, dose-response relationship between childhood trauma and adverse health outcomes across the life course. What the ACE literature has not fully resolved is the mechanism by which that relationship operatesspecifically, why individuals exposed to chronic stress adopt particular behavioral patterns, why those patterns are functionally rational even when socially destructive, and why removing a single behavior without addressing its underlying cause predictably produces a replacement behavior. This paper proposes the Fear Response Gap as an integrative theoretical framework to address these questions. The gap is defined as the neurobiological space created when the fear response feedback loop fails to return to homeostasis-a condition produced by chronic activation of the HPA axis under toxic stress. When the loop cannot close naturally, the organism seeks gap-filling behaviors. Drawing on a framework developed through fourteen years of applied observation in Alaska Native health and governance settings, and grounded in the convergence of Lean Management gap analysis with Felitti's self-healing formulation, this paper formalizes three mechanisms of behavioral adaptation: stacking (the accumulation of multiple gap-filling behaviors as stress burden increases), swapping (temporary substitution when a preferred behavior is unavailable), and switching (permanent behavioral substitution when a behavior becomes inaccessible or too costly). These mechanisms operate across a three-part valence taxonomy-positive-appearing, tolerable-appearing, and destructive-appearing behaviors-that reframes so-called negative behavior as rational gap-filling rather than pathology or moral failure. The paper further introduces the threshold variable as the bidirectional dynamic property governing movement within the tolerable-appearing stack, the minimum relational container as the floor condition required for gap closure, and the DOSE-seeking framework (dopamine, oxytocin, serotonin, endorphin) as the neurochemical mechanism underlying behavioral selection. Implications for intervention design, Indigenous community health, and the limits of symptomfocused treatment are discussed. The framework was developed from inside a Shangukeidí clan epistemological position and was first operationalized as an organizational strategy at Chugachmiut in 2010-2012, prior to its theoretical formalization. This paper provides the theoretical foundation for a cluster of companion papers that apply the framework to community surveillance (Anderson, 2026b), suicide prevention (Anderson, 2026c), criminal sentencing reform (Anderson, 2026d), and organizational improvement (Anderson, 2026a).

detail.abstract: Choosing how easy to make it for buyers to discover new sellers is a key design decision for platforms. On the one hand, enabling more discoverability generates more transactions and can be more attractive for sellers because they anticipate being discovered by new buyers. On the other hand, discoverability can make sellers more reluctant to participate because they anticipate their existing buyers will discover and purchase from other sellers. We model this fundamental tradeoff and study how a platform's optimal level of discoverability depends on various factors: the degree of substitutability between the sellers' products, the standalone value of the platform's tools, the size of the platform's installed base of buyers, the nature of the platform's fees including its ability to charge differential fees depending on whether a transaction is with a seller's existing buyers or not, the number of sellers, and asymmetries between sellers' sizes.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a formal framework for a strategic phenomenon that is widely recognized by practitioners across competitive domains but has not been codified in game theory: the intragame regime shift from value-building play to variance-reducing play under a fixed winmaximization objective. I define the Strategic Transition Region (STR) as the band of game states within which a rational agent's optimal policy undergoes an observable structural change. Not because its objective function has changed, but because the relationship between accumulated advantage and win probability has entered a region of diminishing marginal returns, causing the argmax structure of the fixed objective to shift from expansive, valueseeking moves to compressive, variance-reducing moves. Drawing on observations from artificial intelligence (notably AlphaGo), competitive games, military strategy, and financial portfolio theory, I argue that this regime shift constitutes a distinct and formalizable strategic event. I characterize the STR, analyze the information it reveals to opponents, and derive the Divergent Response Principle: the counterintuitive result that the optimal response to a detected regime shift is variance-seeking rather than mirroring. I further examine the possibility of a false signal (or bluffed) transition as a meta-strategic instrument. I propose that this framework, which I term Strategic Transition Theory (STT), warrants formal codification as a complement to existing equilibria and solution concepts in game theory.

detail.abstract: A key issue for the design of online marketplaces is addressing leakage. Buyers may use the marketplace to discover a seller or to obtain certain conveniences, but the seller may then want to take transactions off the marketplace to avoid transaction fees. Assuming buyers are heterogenous in their switching cost or inconvenience cost of purchasing directly, we provide a model in which there is partial leakage in equilibrium. We use the model to analyze the tradeoffs associated with different strategies the marketplace can use to attenuate the effects of leakage: investing in transaction benefits, limiting communication, charging referral fees, using price-parity clauses, introducing seller competition on the marketplace and hiding sellers that try to induce too much leakage.

detail.abstract: As climate change raises temperatures and the US elderly population swells from 12 to 17 percent of the population between 2000 and 2024, two forces are pulling American public health in opposite directions. Hotter summers threaten cardiovascular health, especially among older adults whose thermoregulatory systems are weakest, yet decades of air conditioning adoption have steadily reduced the mortality impact of extreme heat. Whether adaptation is outpacing this rapid demographic shift remains an open question. This paper answers it using 25 years of county-level data on age-specific cardiovascular mortality, temperature, and demographics across 3,135 US counties. I exploit within-county weather variation in a triple-difference design that compares how elderly and working-age mortality respond to heat shocks, and how that differential evolves over time. The results are clear: the elderly are adapting. Under the most demanding specification, which absorbs state-by-year-by-age fixed effects, a one-standard-deviation heat shock closes the elderly-young mortality gap by 1.3 deaths per 100,000 more each year than it did at the start of the sample. Adaptation among older Americans has outpaced the mechanical increase in vulnerability from population aging. Critically, the speed of adaptation depends on energy costs. In states where electricity is cheaper, elderly heat vulnerability has fallen faster, pointing to residential air conditioning as the primary protective technology. This finding reframes energy assistance programs such as the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program: they are not merely antipoverty transfers but function as climate adaptation policy for an aging population.

detail.abstract: We explore conditions under which a multiproduct firm can profitably turn itself into a platform by "hosting rivals," i.e. by inviting rivals to sell products or services on top of its core product. Hosting eliminates the additional shopping costs to consumers of buying a specialist rival's competing version of the multiproduct firm's non-core product. On the one hand, this makes it easier for the rival to compete on the non-core product. On the other hand, hosting turns the rival from a pure competitor into a complementor: the value added by its product now helps raise consumer demand for the multi-product firm's core product. As a result, hosting can be both unilaterally profitable for the multi-product firm and jointly profitable for both firms.

detail.abstract: The efficacy of international sanctions in bringing about compliance with the goals of the sender is of interest to both International Relations (IR) and development scholars. Yet, aid suspensions receive less attention in sanctions research than economic sanctions, which may be biasing our understanding of sanctions efficacy. Since recent research has established that different autocratic types display diverging degrees of resilience to sanctions, we ascertain whether such claims are applicable to aid suspensions. First, we look at how resilient different regime types are to sanctions and then investigate whether results for aid suspensions differ from those for sanctions in general. After that, we hypothesise that wealth protects autocracies less from aid suspensions than from other sanctions because their effects are harder to evade. With the help of econometric analysis, we test our hypotheses on original data that feature aid suspensions as a stand-alone category. Test results corroborate the superior resistance of single-party regimes and monarchies. A final test on the role of target prosperity uncovers a nuance: affluence strengthens target resistance to economic sanctions but not to aid suspensions. This confirms our evasion hypothesis: while alternative trade routes can offset a ban on trade with a set of senders, substitute donors are rare.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the collateral mortality benefits of South Korea's nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) against COVID-19 on deaths from non-COVID-19 respiratory diseases. Utilizing a Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) model, we constructed a synthetic control group using non-respiratory causes of death, such as malignant neoplasms and chronic non-communicable diseases. Our analysis of national cause-of-death statistics from January 2016 to December 2023 revealed a significant divergence between observed and counterfactual mortality during the intensive intervention period of 2020-2022. The results indicate that non-COVID-19 respiratory mortality decreased by approximately 23% relative to the expected baseline, representing an estimated 49,831 avoided deaths. The validity of this causal inference was confirmed through two placebo tests: one substituting leukemia as a non-communicable outcome and another artificially setting the intervention date to January 2019. These findings demonstrate that measures designed to contain SARS-CoV-2 effectively interrupted the transmission of concurrent respiratory pathogens, generating substantial public health co-benefits beyond direct viral containment. Consequently, future pandemic cost-benefit analyses should account for this collateral preservation of lives from secondary respiratory threats.

detail.abstract: Despite large potential cost savings, firms frequently underinvest in energy efficiency. We examine whether mandatory information acquisition, absent public disclosure or required action, can change this behavior. Using the United Kingdom's Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme which requires firms to conduct independent energy assessments but does not require implementation or disclosure of the identified recommendations, we study the real effects of information-based interventions. Employing a difference-in-differences design, we find that mandatory energy assessments lead to reductions in greenhouse gas emissions intensity. Additional analyses point to two channels. First, an information channel, whereby independent assessment reduces uncertainty around carbon-reduction investments, improves understanding of energy use, and provides relevant inputs for decision-making. Second, a salience channel, whereby the assessment process increases the visibility and perceived importance of energy use, directing managerial attention and increasing internal pressure to act. Our findings show that mandatory energy assessments can meaningfully influence firms' climate change-related behavior.

keywords: and Governance Challenges for U.S. Critical Infrastructure Artificial Intelligence (AI)

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly emerging as a transformative tool in the protection of U.S. critical infrastructure, which includes energy, healthcare, transportation, and financial systems. As cyberattacks become more frequent, sophisticated, and disruptive, AI offers unique opportunities to strengthen national defense by enhancing threat detection, automating incident response, and predicting system vulnerabilities before they escalate into crises. Machine learning algorithms can analyze vast amounts of network traffic to identify anomalies, while AI-driven simulations can model attack scenarios and improve resilience planning. Yet the very integration of AI into cyber defense introduces significant risks. Adversarial AI techniques, such as data poisoning and algorithm manipulation, can weaponize the technology against the systems it was designed to protect. Overreliance on automated decision-making may reduce human oversight and accountability, while black-box algorithms raise profound challenges for transparency, due process, and ethical governance in national security contexts. Moreover, AI systems themselves create new attack surfaces, exposing critical infrastructure to cascading failures across interconnected sectors. This dual-use dilemma underscores the urgent need for comprehensive policy and regulatory frameworks that balance innovation with safeguards. Current U.S. initiatives, including efforts by CISA, NIST, and the Department of Defense, provide a foundation, yet gaps remain when compared to emerging international standards such as the EU AI Act. This paper employs a comparative and socio-legal approach to analyze the opportunities and risks of AI in cyber defense, drawing on case studies in power grids, healthcare systems, and transportation networks. It argues for a multi-layered strategy that combines AI innovation with robust human oversight, legal accountability, and public-private collaboration. By placing the "law on trial" in the digital domain, this study calls for integrated technological, legal, and ethical approaches to secure U.S. critical infrastructure in the age of artificial intelligence.

detail.title: How will we use our time in a future of sustainable wellbeing?
detail.abstract: Time use analysis is an accessible and intuitive method for building an understanding of the greenhouse gas emissions footprint of lifestyles, and the ways in which these lifestyles impact our enjoyment and wellbeing. This study develops a novel methodology to estimate the emissions footprint and wellbeing of lifestyles in 2050 in three global north countries (Finland, France, and the UK) from a time use perspective. This modelling utilises time use analysis, wellbeing data, direct emissions data, environmentally extended multiregional input-output analysis (MRIO), and scenario building. We first construct an ambitious 2050 scenario assuming a move to sufficiency-based household consumption of commodities and energy, dietary change, systemic changes to transport habits, technological change and cleaner production, and energy efficiency improvements. Despite modelling these ambitious changes out to 2050, we estimate that the emissions intensity of global north lifestyles will remain outside planetary boundaries. We then model the specific wellbeing and emissions in three time use scenarios, or ’lifestyles’, for all three countries to understand how time use changes can improve wellbeing and lower lifestyle emissions. These scenarios are shaped by insights from functional time use theory (FTU), with further insights from the provisioning systems literature. We find that, though it is possible to improve our wellbeing and lower emissions through lifestyle change, further radical transformations are required to provisioning systems to bring emissions footprints within planetary boundaries. Moreover, without this transformation, some socially positive changes to time use may have unintended negative environmental effects.
